newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy sees swift decision on Albania force.
newsitem.headline: Italy sees swift decision on Albania force.

text.p: Italy said on Tuesday that it expected a decision to be taken "within days" on the size and aims of a foreign protection force that would be sent to Albania to guard a European Union relief mission.
But Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, speaking after EU foreign ministers met Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino in Rome, insisted Italy would not intervene on its own in the chaos-hit Balkan state.

"We are preparing with other countries a multilateral security force to give security protection to civilians we are sending with the European Union to Albania," Dini told a news conference. "We don't intend to...operate on our own."
A decision on the size of the force would be taken in the next few days. "Its dimensions will depend on the objectives which it is set," Dini said.

Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said Madrid was ready in principle to join such a force and non-EU member Turkey has also expressed willingness. Dini said Austria and Romania, another non-EU state, were also prepared to take part.

EU foreign ministers meeting in Brussels on Monday again shied away from backing military intervention in Albania, where large areas of the south are out of government control and in the hands of armed rebels and lawless mafias.

But they welcomed the efforts of certain EU states to assemble a force "under the appropriate international aegis" to provide security for the delivery of food and medical relief to the impoverished Balkan state.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country holds the EU presidency, said an advisory team -- the second in as many weeks -- would leave for Albania on Wednesday to assess the scale of the planned relief mission.
The 54-member Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is regarded by countries ready to commit forces to the mission as the appropriate forum to give the go-ahead.
But Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel of Germany, which has said it will not send troops, told reporters that he believed a United Nations mandate was desirable.
He also made clear that EU countries in general were not willing to become involved in another Bosnia-style quagmire.
"Europe is unanimous that it is not right to send soldiers on a large scale to Albania," Kinkel said in Rome.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind also highlighted the distaste for intervention, saying adequate security for an EU relief mission need not be large.
"To send an army to Albania would risk becoming involved in the internal affairs of what is a very unstable country. That would be unwise and does not seem to be necessary," he said.

Italy has been at the forefront of international efforts to resolve the unrest, which Rome says is now being used as an excuse by Albanians to head for a better life in a flotilla of rundown boats that have docked at its southeastern ports.

Dini signed a bilateral accord with Albanian Foreign Minister Arjan Starova on Tuesday that allows for blanket Italian naval patrols of the Adriatic to block an exodus that has already brought 12,000 Albanians to Italy since March 13.
He said the aim, shared by Albania, was to conduct "strict patrolling with the intention of sending back every ship and boat that turns up" and was not carrying genuine refugees.
